query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, degradation of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA is governed by the formation and integrity of a continuous, thin Al/Ti-rich oxide scale that forms only under oxidizing conditions. This protective scale retards oxygen ingress and preserves the fcc matrix, whereas under reducing conditions the lack of a robust oxide layer leads to internal oxidation and microstructural destabilization.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 in an as-fabricated, fully fcc matrix state with high strength and fatigue resistance.
generation.intervention: Expose identical alloy samples to controlled elevated-temperature environments (e.g., 750 °C) in either oxidizing gas (e.g., air) or a reducing gas environment (e.g., H2-diluted inert gas) for varying time durations.
generation.conditions: Temperature around 750 °C with exposure durations sufficient to promote scale formation (e.g., 10–50 hours), and controlled gas compositions representing distinctly oxidizing versus reducing environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation (or lack) of an adherent, continuous Al/Ti-rich oxide scale on the alloy surface that mediates oxygen diffusion into the bulk and influences internal microstructural stability.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, selective oxidation of the available Al and Ti produces a protective oxide layer that limits further oxygen ingress and preserves the matrix integrity. Under reducing conditions, the absence or instability of this protective layer permits more rapid internal oxygen penetration, promoting degradation through internal oxidation and potential phase destabilization.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed to the oxidizing environment will show formation of a thin, continuous Al/Ti-rich oxide scale with limited internal oxidation and minimal loss of mechanical properties, whereas samples in reducing atmospheres will exhibit a more heterogeneous or incomplete oxide formation, increased internal oxidation, and accelerated degradation of strength and fatigue resistance relative to the as-fabricated baseline.
generation.baseline: The as-built alloy state, characterized by a single-phase fcc structure with high strength and fatigue performance prior to any elevated-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies in the elevated-temperature regime (around 750 °C) over extended exposure times (10–50 hours) where gas-phase chemistry is the primary variable; it may not hold at lower temperatures or under transient thermal conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While the selective oxidation of Al and Ti is a plausible mechanism, the precise kinetics of oxide scale formation and the susceptibility to internal oxidation under reducing conditions remain to be quantified. The magnitude of protective effects versus the rate of degradation under reducing media is also uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy samples. Expose one set to an oxidizing environment (air) and the other to a reducing environment (e.g., H2-inert mixture) at 750 °C for durations spanning 10, 25, and 50 hours. After exposure, perform detailed surface analyses (SEM/EDS, XRD) to characterize oxide scale formation, and conduct mechanical testing (hardness, fatigue, tensile strength tests) to assess degradation.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness, continuity, and composition (via SEM/EDS, XRD)
Mechanical property degradation relative to the as-fabricated baseline (hardness, tensile strength, fatigue resistance)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both oxidizing and reducing exposure conditions yield similar oxide scale characteristics and corresponding degradation in mechanical properties, or if the oxidizing environment fails to produce a continuous, protective Al/Ti-rich oxide scale, then the hypothesis that protective oxide formation governs degradation will be falsified.

Microstructure-Property Correlation and Its Evolution during Aging in an Al4.4Co26Cr19Fe18Ni27Ti5.6 High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractThe efficient energy use in multiple sectors of modern industry is partly based on the efficient use of high-strength, high-performance alloys that retain remarkable mechanical properties at elevated and high temperatures. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) represent the most recent class of these materials with a high potential for high-temperature high-strength applications. Aside from their chemical composition and microstructure-property relationship, limited information on the effect of heat treatment as a decisive factor for alloy design is available in the literature. This work intends to contribute to this research topic by investigating the effect of heat treatment on the microstructure and mechanical performance of an Al4.4Co26Cr19Fe18Ni27Ti5.6 HEA. The solution annealed state is compared to aged states obtained at different heat treatment times at 750 °C. Integrated design of aluminum-enriched high-entropy refractory B2 alloys with synergy of high strength and ductility

Abstract: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are promising high-temperature structural materials. Their large compositional space poses great design challenges for phase control and high strength-ductility synergy. The present research pioneers using integrated high-throughput machine learning with Monte Carlo simulations supplemented by ab initio calculations to effectively navigate phase selection and mechanical property predictions, developing single-phase ordered B2 aluminum-enriched RHEAs (Al-RHEAs) demonstrating high strength and ductility. These Al-RHEAs achieve remarkable mechanical properties, including compressive yield strengths up to 1.7 gigapascals, fracture strains exceeding 50%, and notable high-temperature strength retention. They also demonstrate a tensile yield strength of 1.0 gigapascals with a ductility of 9%, albeit with B2 ordering. Enhancing the Elevated-Temperature Mechanical Properties of Levitation Melted NbMoTaW Refractory High-Entropy Alloys via Si Addition

Abstract: To enhance the mechanical properties of NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), Si was added at varying concentrations (x = 0, 0.25, and 0.5) via vacuum induction levitation melting (re-melted six times for homogeneity). The microstructure and mechanical properties of NbMoTaWSix (x = 0, 0.25, and 0.5) RHEAs were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), universal testing, microhardness testing, and tribological equipment. Experimental results manifested that Si addition induces the formation of the (Nb,Ta)5Si3 phase, and the volume fraction of the silicide phase increases with higher Si content, which significantly improves the alloy’s strength and hardness but deteriorates its plasticity. Enhanced wear resistance with Si addition is attributed to improved hardness and oxidation resistance. Tribological tests confirm that Si3N4 counterfaces are optimal for evaluating RHEA wear mechanisms. This work can provide guidance for the fabrication of RHEAs with excellent performance.

Synthesis of Refractory High-Entropy Alloy WTaMoNbV by Powder Bed Fusion Process Using Mixed Elemental Alloying Powder

Abstract: AbstractThe growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process.
